At long last, you approach the location of your many visions.Before you you see an enormous golden sphere. While it's the size of a large asteroid, you're certain it is not a natural formation. As you stare at the strange object, you find your senses stunned and your reason stupified. Who could have built such a thing? And why?You find yourself compelled to get closer to the surface of the object. To touch it's surface. But you feel equally a palpable dread, a stupifying fear of the unknown and impossible.

You spacewalk to the object, feeling an ever growing sense of terror the closer you get. The surface is a gossamer knit weave of golden threads pulled taut and rigid to the touch. Above you is a platform sticking out of the sphere, the only irregularity to the curve of the object. You float to it and see a strange interface above the platform. A hexagonal pillar beside a hexagonal hole. You take the pillar from the surface and hold it in your hand.
Overwhelmed by terror, you decide to leave the strange object. For now.

The golden weave loosens before you and begins to open. The hole before you reveals a bright purple light, and as it grows larger you see there is a shimmering liquid inside of the same color. The opening grows and grows, eventually becomes as large as your ship.You have a vision of an infinite plane suddenly pockmarked with other purple nodes in a network, of which this is just one. You feel a sublime expansive terror, as if you are an ant on an anthill and the camera zooms out and you realize your world is tiny in comparison. You have a terrrible certainty that suddenly you are being observed by trillions of eyes, and most of them are curious. Many of them are coming. Very soon. Perhaps now.

Following a feeling of naive optimism and a willingness to risk one's own life, you enter the sphere. You know that humanity is flawed, failing, but has an ineffable essence that should expand and continue. Going through, even if it kills you personally, is worth it. You find yourself in a bureaucratic metaphysical switchboard  in which you must imagine your ship's essence.You blink to ... somewhere? Silence. You hear your ship nav pan sound but it is panning like crazy, faster and faster as it scrolls out to your new location, lightyears away.

Following a perfectly rational pessimism and a drive to protect one's own life, you wait and see who arrives. You're certain Humanity is failing itself. It can no longer be trusted to decide its own fate. Anything coming through must be better than what we got. Let Daddy come home and sort it out for us. The Entity comes through and asks you "Are you Merga?" Before you can answer, and without any emotion, The Entity harvests all of humanity in the blink of an eye. You enter a dead system as the only remaining human in the universe.

The Object grows larger in your scope with each passing day.You find yourself watching it for hours. You studied the readouts, the videos, the decades of identical reports made by astronomers assigned to observe it. Those methods became insufficient. The optics suite has an eyepiece which, when you look through it, is as close as possible to the unfiltered image captured in the hull-mounted scopes. You keep your eye fixed to that scope until you fall asleep in your chair, and then you watch it in your dreams.In moments of lucidity you realise you are losing track of time. When you are not watching the Object, you're tending to the needs of your ship, and those of your own body, in that order. When those are taken care of, you return to the scope. A rational part of your brain observes that this is not healthy or safe or particularly sane. Unfortunately, your rational brain is fully on board with the irrational parts of your brain telling you to watch the Object, and these observations are abandoned as quickly as they're made.It's not like there's anything interesting to watch. From any distance it is the same uniform circle. A child's drawing of a gold coin, or the closed eye of a sleeping dragon. You might as well be watching the O2 light on the NAV console; it's a similarly amber-coloured LED that, should it ever change to red, would convey the information that you are about to die. That would be something.But you return to your position at the scope; what is interesting for you and what is not has become irrelevant.

A revelation! You're no longer confined to your seat at the scope. This is because the image of the Object at 79AU has burned into your retina. That's your best explanation for how you can always see it, even while you're doing inconsequential things like eating or going to the toilet. This has freed up your hours aboard the ship, and in the nick of time too, for several runaway processes were leading to a total breakdown, both in the ship's systems and your own. You're able to put most of them to rights.You try to get a few hours a day at the scope to keep your hand in, but that's only because you're an overachiever.Your ship has pushed deep into the Kuiper Belt. You receive mail from the scant human souls who've ventured out here. It's mostly friendly, but it dries up once word gets around that you don't reply. Afterwards you get the occasional ping curious about what you're doing, or where you're headed, or sad to see you go. You get a heartfelt message from, if the header is to be believed, the only Trans-Neptunian psychiatrist.You try to write back about the Object that has eclipsed your vision, but as you put metaphorical pen to paper, it all falls apart. Reading your drafts back, it's as if another writer has surreptitiously accessed the document and muddled your thoughts. You can't include any of it in a reply. You'd look insane.

The Object is quite the conversationalist. Silly you, thinking it was mute. You hadn't learned its language. It took a little mental adjustment, a bit like training yourself to speak your native tongue back to front. That hurdle overcome, you find the Object verbally adroit, suave, quick with a joke, and equally content to play the listener.Would you have ever believed that there are higher orders of physics, natural laws that you're the only human ever to appreciate? The Object would have. Indeed, it helped you find them, even encouraged you to name a few after yourself. Not all of them - future explorers should be allowed to share that honour. In hindsight it's hard to understand the furore on Ceres over a cheap party trick like teleportation. The secrets you're privy to would bring nations to their knees, on your personal order, no less. You clear one room of your ship and dedicate it to your studies, conducting experiments and assays into new forms of physicalised thought, splicing axiom and aphorism before ducking behind a mental blast shield in case they explode, as they occasionally do, into real flames.The Object is your capable assistant throughout, studiously copying your dictations to paper on its clipboard. The Object's negligence is revealed as wisdom. It's saving you from yourself. You know there's no need to thank it. You're colleagues in a shared scholarly tradition. This is what it is to have a peer.

The Object leaves you as the torch drive goes cold.It's been days since you've spoken aloud to it, or it to you. "Exegetic," you say. You hope that not all the aliens you meet will be this dead set on five dollar words."79 AU," says Joakim, "is a Class 13 deep space communications probe of disputed ownership. It has five rainbows transmission, 9th generation intersimulation technology, and over one megabytes of addressable memory, suitable for First Contact, Last Contact, and everything in between. In honour of its eight thousand years of service, including service with distinction in the War Of Two Monads, it appears in gold, a Baryonic element and spectrum of light many cultures associate with the divine."You frown. "One megabyte?"Joakim frowns back. "Excuse me," he says, thinking for a second. "Signed integer overflow. I could start listing zeroes but we'd be here all day."

"Exigent.""It's your last chance," says Joakim. His air of calculated weirdness is gone. "The Wall is coming down. The enclave will engulf. How? How is your why. It's up to you."Not for the first time, you're confronted by a monumental concept which evokes no strong reaction from you. You shake your head. "I'm not sure I can make that choice.""That's the kind of thing you should avoid saying," he says, "unless you want to trigger the worst possible outcome."
Can you tell me the other thing you said?

"What?""I offered you two perfectly good options there," Joakim says, "and you went with 'what?'""Um," you say. "Yes." That is, after all, what happened."Then I'm going to give you some free advice," he continues. "You'll get exactly what you ask for. If you ask for nothing, you'll get nothing.""Can I choose one of them now," you ask hopefully, "'exhibit' or whatever?""No," he says.
The elevator admits you, the chair jolting uncomfortably as you cross the gap.You have perfect recall of Joakim's information. Where do you want to go?

Smooth as anaesthetic wearing off, the next thing you're aware of is you, lying in a bed.You awaken slowly, wrapped in soft cotton. A machine beeps to let you know you're alright.You're in a medical bed surrounded by diagnostic equipment. You are not, however, in a hospital ward. The bed and equipment - you look around slowly, serenely - are in a hotel lobby. It's functional, modern, glass and marble, neutral colours, a transitional style.At the far end of the lobby, lifts travel up and down a transparent shaft. Closer, doors lead from the lobby to adjoining wings. The one with signage near enough to read, written across an arch above the door, says 'Pool'.Much closer is the front desk. A man stands at ease behind it. He returns your gaze, but gives no other acknowledgement.

You hear the music before the elevator has even reached the first floor. When the doors part you're hit by a wall of sound, and sympathetic vibrations rattle the chair.You wheel through the hall past empty rooms to 103. Even if it were unlabeled, and it isn't, the door rattling in its frame is a dead giveaway that somebody is home.Uncertain how a knock could be heard, no alternatives spring to mind, so you knock. The music turns down sharply, then sharply again, as someone hurriedly turns a volume knob. You hear whispers. Then a bright voice, a man's: "Come in!"You hesitate. Women's voices harmonise in a major third: "It's open!"You push the door open.

A generous soul would call the room bohemian. A miserly soul would call it a mess.In the centre stand a group of black megaliths, which at second glance are hi-fi speakers. Piled around them is dilapidated furniture, low-slung couches and divans, and cushions on the lam. Piled on top of all that is a sedimentary layer of takeout food containers, empty record sleeves, and paperback novels. The room has a pungent, verdant aroma. It's not unpleasant, but it is impossible to ignore.The occupants leap up, excited to see you. "Come in, come in!" they cry. "Do you want something to eat? Drink? Cool cast, man!"They seem human. Sanguine, a tall thin man with a sensitive face and a pencil moustache, got first billing from Joakim, but seems not to talk so much. Most of the talking is done by Emerald, an intense woman with an unambiguous colour scheme. Fire, wearing red, wanders over to a divan and lays down, and says little after that. "She smoked too much," says Emerald. "Don't worry about her.""We're so happy to meet a human in the flesh!" she continues. "Are you from Earth? Who's your favourite Beatle?""Let them breathe, Em," says Sanguine. He's wearing a powder blue suit. "Humans need to breathe.""I'm not from Earth," you say. "I'm from Ganymed Ten Thirty Six.""Oh," she says. "Is that near Earth?""Sometimes," you say."Cool," she says, derailed. "... anyway we love Earth music! We loved your record. Amazing stuff on there. All over the place conceptually, but it put us on to some of your less mainstream artists, and then we got it!""Record?" you say. "What record?""The Golden Record," she says, as if it's crazy you've never heard of it. "By Voyager 1."

"You're aliens," you say."That's right," says Emerald.You're unable to be amazed. The closest you can get is credulous. "What is an alien?""It's often hard to say," says Sanguine. "In the interstellar, it helps to have an open mind.""You three," you say. "Are you a race, a species, a society? How many of you are there? Is everyone at the hotel one of you?""Steady on!" says Emerald. "Yes, yes, it's complicated, we don't know, and no. What Sanguine means is, set aside assumptions. In your planetary system, physical feedback loops developed into an individualistic spacefaring society. You're relatively rare! You shouldn't expect to meet, oh," she casts around, looking to Sanguine for support, "bipedal humanoids much like yourself with just a few cardinal differences.""Which isn't to say those don't exist," says Sanguine. "But subluminals tend to stick to their own, um," he says. "Context? Birthright?""Homeworld," moans Fire."You know that's not right," says Emerald crossly. "You're only going to confuse the poor thing.""It's good enough for now," says Fire, and rolls over so her back is to the rest of you.

"If you had to pick one or two differences to distinguish you from me," you say, "what would they be?""Oh, very well," says Emerald. "You take this one. I'm going to fix us drinks."Sanguine cocks his head, and leads you to one edge of the room, where tall glass doors open onto a balcony. Beyond the balcony is empty space, and the Milky Way. You roll outside cautiously."Let's get some air," he says. It's a joke about the vacuum, which you find breathable. "We need clear heads. If you were desperate to label us, you could call us Aesthetes. Do you know what teleology is?"You shake your head. "It's a Greek word," he says, "for investigating the purposes of things. A useful concept. We search for experiences, for novelty. That's who we are and what we do. When we heard Voyager 1, it was a glorious day. There's a whole galaxy out there aching to hear that quintessentially human sound, you dig?"

"I was beginning to think my way of life was done for," you say. "Most of the aliens I've met are indifferent or hostile. But you guys seem cool.""Thank you for saying that," Sanguine says sincerely. He speaks with a quiet drawl, and his voice is inviting, like he's always sharing good news with you. "Not everyone is sympatico.""If you were to be the, uhm," you say, "stewards for humanity, I guess? Would you take care of us?"He shakes his head sadly. "No can do, amigo. We want to preserve that unique thing you've got going on, but the other ententes won't let that happen.""Shit," you say. "For a second I thought things might be easy."He smiles and claps your shoulder. "Our credo rebels against 'easy'. Too boring for us." He turns to the sea of stars, leaning on the balcony. The riotous band of purple and orange has never looked brighter. "You made it this far. I'm sure you'll figure something out."
That sounds like a good option

"I like the sound of that," you say. "How do you join? Is it an open club?""It is," he says slowly, "yes. But.""But?""But what you're asking is not what you think you're asking," he says. "Experience is, I learned this one recently, a 'two way street'. This is why we don't like labels. Becoming something other than human means exactly that."You look down at your mending body, the wheelchair you need to move around. "I wouldn't be human anymore."He sighs - not frustrated, but he was anticipating you would say that. "Yes and no! That's what I'm getting at.""Do you know what a leap of faith is?" you ask. He nods. "Is it like that?" He nods again. "Got it."

The Milky Way is a timely reminder of the vast difference between an empirical understanding of reality, which most people including yourself subscribed to by default, and the milieu in which you currently find yourself. You're among interstellar beings advanced enough to take human form and make themselves approachable, downright urbane. How to conceive of this? Are they made of atoms? Are you?"The more I walk this path," you say to Sanguine, "the less real it seems. That's frightening." You take a straw poll of your emotional state, and find it unchanged. "Even if I'm not frightened, I think I should be," you add."That's life, man," he says. "It's a constant process of growing too comfortable, having that illusion shatter, and rebuilding it over from square one.""But whenever my understanding broadens," you say, "it diminishes everything that came before. There's nothing to hold on to."He gestures at himself, his blue suit and his unassuming, gangly figure. "You probably don't think I'm a fighter. I am. We're fighting every day. You have to fight for yourself. The universe will destroy you if you let it. Get past the alienation, the dissociation, and hold on to what you can."He drums his fingers on the rail. The lights of the Milky Way are huge and luminous reflected in his eyes. "It's terribly beautiful out here," he says. "I'm glad we came."

A tray of tinkling glasses announces the return of Emerald. You follow Sanguine back inside, and he shuts the glass partition behind you."Is this an interstellar favourite?" you ask hopefully. "Something they drink across the galaxy?"Emerald sets your glass next to you, embarrassed. It's a familiar black liquid. "Bacardi and Coke," she says. "Our hats off to the Cubans and the Coca-Cola company."

"This is all coming across as matter-of-fact," you say. "I can't give it the reaction it deserves.""This place has a different energy than you're used to," says Emerald. She looks at Sanguine, who nods in encouragement. "It'll give you a synthetic perspective." That's not a combination of words you can parse."They're asking about the substrate," says Fire from the divan, eyes shut, words muffled by a pillow. "Tell them about the substrate.""Oh yes!" says Emerald. "In this place, non-Baryonic elements can intermediate with your own matter. Modulated gold and what you call 'void opal' catalyse a harmonic environment that suits us both."More technobabble, to be honest. "Am I supposed to understand that?""No," says Sanguine. "But we don't talk down to folks in First Contact. Honesty is the best policy."
Interrogate your own lack of reaction

"You look like me," you say. "Human.""Thank you!" says Emerald. "That's really a very great compliment.""Why don't you look like," you ask haltingly, "what you normally look like?"Emerald hesitates as if you're speaking another language. She looks to Sanguine. He leans forward. "This is what we normally look like," he says. Unspoken communication passes between him and Sanguine. "This place translates for us. It translates everything.""Can you show me your true forms?" you ask. A look of shock passes across Emerald's face, quickly suppressed."I don't think so, no," she says. "For everybody's sake."

"You found the Voyager probe?""Sure did," says Emerald. "Lucky 79 AU happened to be going this way. We'd never have noticed it otherwise.""All our broadcasts," you say, "our radio waves flooding interstellar space. Nobody heard them?""There's not a lot going on in this cluster, and radio's not in vogue. Give it, oh," she pauses. "A few thousand years." She pats your knee encouragingly. "Someone'll hear Arecibo, you see if they don't!"
Pick apart their recent cosmic history

With only the four of you it's an intimate gathering, but you find time for yourself. The others leave you be as you idly rummage through their record diaspora. You're not sure what you're hunting for, exactly, but with such an eclectic range, they're sure to have it. The big squares seem to be envelopes for gratuitously large discs, one of which you can see turning on an open-faced disc player, which is propped up on a pile of detective novels.You flip past names like the Beatles, Miles Davis, Parliament Funkadelic, Invisible Acropolis. You only recognise the Beatles, and infer they must be great artists from their age.Under an empty pizza box you find names you recognise from when you were a kid. There's a lot of generic klaxpop. They have both of Dalisay's releases from her brief pivot from acting to singing, and they might be alone in the universe for that. They have a couple of mash records, but much more from the subgenre that killed it in the 2060s, smash.One of the records is addressed to you. "For [us-firstname]," it says. You're there, pictured on the cover. The artist listed is 'Isambard Cruz'.

You go to the record player and remove the disc from its spindle, replacing it with the one bearing your name and face. The conversation peters out. You replace the tonearm. It settles into the groove."Hello again, [us-firstname]. You remember me: Isambard Cruz. Happy to find you with friends of mine. You are safe but not long now. I hope Ben is alright. Too much happening, too fast.""79 AU called for a long time. At last someone answer. You. Hoped not for your sake, hoped yes for mine.""Earth doomed itself. Nothing we can do there. Can save Earth's children. Speak for us. Someone must.""Time of false-facing will pass. When there are no barriers, we rejoin our shadows. Another night. Another day."She coughs. It's wet, not the cough of a healthy person. "The cloud is humming. I hear it. Hope you hear it too.""Take care of yourself, [us-firstname]. Make sure you eat properly."It ends in pops and crackles of dead air.

Like all experienced partiers, the Aesthetes know to leave while the going is good.You find yourself at the door, hovering on the threshold, as you all say your goodbyes. "This was fun," says Sanguine. "You're welcome any time.""Don't be a stranger!" says Emerald."In fact hold on," says Sanguine, and disappears for a moment. He returns with one of the pizza boxes so crammed full of leftovers that the lid can't close. "Someone needs to eat these. Please take it. You'd be doing us a favour."You refuse as graciously as possible, and then it's a short roll to the elevator.Who are we, in these interstitial moments, between the closing of a door and a solitary journey back the way we came? They don't stick in memory. Before the return of our self-regard, when the party's concluded, it's as if we don't exist.

What was it Joakim said? The "basement" is full of "terrestrial emanations". It seems like something you should investigate. After all, you're terrestrial.The elevator shaft descends into an environment that, as you scope it through the glass panes, you're immediately familiar with: it shares the mien of every hold, bay, storage compartment - generally any place for dumping stuff you don't want - that you've ever visited, used, or at some stage lived in. They don't build basements in space, but they're there in spirit.Its surfaces are smooth concrete. Set into the walls are wide metal doors with a diagonal seam, a combination digital and mechanical lock in their centre.The elevator descends into a corridor junction that seems to go on forever. Far as the eye can see, there is concrete and doors, doors and concrete.

You roll yourself out of the elevator before you notice someone lounging against the call button, a human woman in navy blue coveralls. A lit cigarette dangles from her fingers."Hello?" you ask. "I'm here about the ... Joakim sent me.""He did, did he," she says. She has clipped hair and, somehow, a clipped expression. "Joakim doesn't do anything. None of the staff do.""Okay, he didn't send me, exactly," you admit. "He listed places I could go and the basement was one of them." You wonder whether you've misunderstood. "If I'm not supposed to be here -""You can be here," she says. She runs a hand across her head. "That's why I've come. Do exactly what I tell you. I represent the warden, and if you break its rules, you'll regret it."

Rules. Good. About time this place had some rules. You voice that thought aloud, and she doesn't laugh. Ah, well. "Come on," she says. She punches a button sequence on a door keypad, then casually shoves the wheel in the centre of the lock. It spins easily out to its fullest extent, and the doors draw back, long diagonal partitions sliding left and right.Inside is a motor pool, with four conical ground cars in various states of maintenance. She goes to the most roadworthy one and, reaching inside the cockpit, heaves, so that it slowly rolls into the corridor while she walks alongside. When it's outside the motor pool she reaches in and engages the brake.It's a deeply unimpressive vehicle. It has no paint job, unless that paint was an uneven grey. Once she has helped you out of your chair and into the back seat, she presses the accelerator, revealing the car is not particularly fast either. The alien designers must have carefully weighed both form and function, and decided to put both last."What happened to the leg?" she asks."I drove my spaceship into it," you say."Ah," she says.You putter along in this crappy vehicle with some time to kill.

"The warden runs a tight ship, huh," you say."Believe it," she says, watching the speedometer, which doesn't change."If you wouldn't mind telling me those rules?""I was going to," she says. "There's no gotchas. Number one, don't talk to anything in a cell. No communication of any kind. Number two, don't disturb the panopticon. Number one is a subset of two. Number three, remain under my supervision at all times.""What happens if I break one?""You get a cell in the panopticon."

The car travels at a perfectly fixed speed, and the shift between wall and door and wall and door grows faintly revolting. You focus instead on the woman in dark blue, who despite paying you no mind is easier on the eyes."You work for the warden?""I am the warden," she says. "You said something different before," you say."I did. That doesn't mean I work for it.""'It' meaning 'you'."."Find someone else to clarify how it works," she says without heat. "My job is to interface with you because the warden can't.""I only asked to make conversation," you say. "Do you have a name?"She looks back at you, a lingering and uncomfortably penetrating stare. "You may call me Ariel," she says at last, and refocuses on the road ahead so that it does not invite a follow up.

"Joakim said you have terrestrial emanations here," you say."Yes.""You're taking me to see them?""Yes," she says. "One.""What is it?""We don't know," she says. It's perhaps the first time she’s revealed vulnerability. "That is probably why Joakim mentioned it."

Ariel stops the car at a door the same as any other. She takes a moment to stretch her legs. You decide it's not worth the hassle to do so yourself. "Refreshments?" she asks. She reaches in to open a glove compartment, which is full of energy bars and DND Cola.You take an energy bar and a drink. Whatever the extraordinary features of 79 AU, it must not keep you fed and watered, or why would they offer? Start the countdown to needing an alien restroom. She pockets an energy bar for herself, and lights up another cigarette.When the break is over, she walks to the door and repeats the opening process. The doors slide apart. Immediately on the other side, there's a transparent divider. You can only tell it's there because you're reflected in it. Through the glass, darkly, there is nothing.You look at her, wondering what it is you're supposed to see.

"Can't see anything?" she asks.You shake your head. "They like to shroud the cell in darkness," she says. "A simple defensive involution protocol. It doesn't know where it is, or what's happening to it. The one-way manifold doesn't exist in there." She raps her knuckles on the glass, which you suppose is not glass at all. "Okay. We've humoured it long enough." She fishes some packages from a pocket on her coveralls. She rips one open and hands it to you. Inside is a disposable pair of glasses. She rips open the other and puts another pair on.She taps the rim of her glasses to demonstrate. "Cycle the scanner. Set it to gamma."You put the glasses on and tap the rim. Your vision is overlaid with familiar blue-cold/red-hot blobs of infrared. The space beyond the glass is blue, or empty - take your pick. You glance at Ariel experimentally, but if she's anything other than human, it's not apparent. Her yellow-hot face tilts at you. You hurriedly tap the glasses and cycle through the spectrum.Passing out one side of radio and arriving back at gamma, there's a change in the room beyond the wall. In its centre there is a faint humanoid outline in white. Within the outline is a white blob which might describe a face. The centre of its chest is a luminous purple. Emerging from the outline is a prickly white aura, stabbing at the darkness around it, peaking and receding like an audio waveform."I see it," you say. Your mouth is suddenly dry."Good," she says approvingly. "What is it?"

"I have no idea," you say."You've never seen one of these before? Or heard about them? No records of it in media, traditional or modern?" You shake your head at each question. "Yeah. That's where I had my money." You open your mouth. "Figure of speech." You shut it.You take off the glasses. The entity's silhouette is not a calming presence. Ariel takes a long drag on her cigarette. "This was a bust, then."

"What do you know about it?" you ask."Not a whole lot," she says. "We can't get close. It has supernatural capabilities, which as best we can tell, it vastly overestimates. Catching them and overpowering them is trivial." A grim smile plays at the edge of her mouth. "They all operate from the same playbook, which was as outdated on First Contact as it is today.""And it came from Earth?" you ask.She tilts her head noncommittally. "Tracing the signal is a dead end, but all the dead ends are on Earth. Besides, it's shaped just like you." She looks at her body. "And currently, me. We put two and two together."
What do you know about it?

"You can't get close to it?" you ask. Feeling particularly out of the loop, you point at the glass. "It's right there.""Silly me," says Ariel. "We never thought to walk up and shake its hand. No, it doesn't want anything to do with us. We tried contact you would find conventional, and we tried ways you would find unpleasant. Sincere attempts to forge a bridge between worlds. All were rejected. The instant we get past defenses they consider vital, we hit a dead man's switch, and we're talking to the void."She puts her hands on her hips, ash flaking off the end of her cigarette. "Embarrassing. It kept happening. We had no idea what we were doing wrong. We were forced to conclude their kind is fundamentally antisocial, paranoid, and arrogant. We had no choice but to shove them in storage."
Why can't you get close to it?

"Joakim said you had hundreds of this thing. Whatever it is.""He did, and we do," she says. She takes a contemplative drag on the cigarette, sizing up her opponent. "Going back a bit, when 79 AU arrived they swarmed us. A hail of arrows from the undergrowth met by sixteen-inch guns. I took no pleasure in it." The cigarette coal flares. A trail of smoke streams from her nostrils. "Since then we'll get one every few years testing our defences. They're all here. Every single one. Alive and unharmed, assuming they entered that way.""Joakim said they were 'free to a good home'." An unpleasant thought, the kind of place this being would consider a good home."We don't want them," says Ariel. "Storage is unlimited, our patience is not."

"Does part of this fact-finding expedition involve me talking to it? I know it's against the rules," you say. "But you're not going to put me in there, are you?"Ariel laughs. "No." And an aftershock laugh, verging on a giggle. "No, that wouldn't help at all."
Do you want me to talk to it?

Following your last exchange of words, her head snaps to the glass. It's the fastest you've seen her move. "Put the glasses on," Ariel says quietly.You put them on. The humanoid outline, which had appeared to stand appreciably far back, is much, much larger; the entity is standing directly on the other side of the wall. It is as close as it can get to you both."What's it doing?" you ask.She doesn't reply."Does it do this often?"Again she doesn't reply. She goes to the locking mechanism and engages it. The doors slide shut. She spins the wheel counterclockwise, and when it stops, she strains against it until it absolutely does not budge.Climbing into the driver's seat, she reaches over her shoulder for the glasses, which you return.

"I suspect that was not good," you say. The car eats up ground at the same frustratingly measured pace. "Maybe even bad," you say to her unresponsive back.Ariel does reply, but it's after a hard thirty seconds of silence. "Hostile entities are kept in panopticon," she says coolly. "For their protection, and ours. If we choose, they can't tell they are being viewed. Observation goes one way, outside-in." She is silent for another long while. "Or so we believed."You can see how that might unsettle an entity styling itself as a warden. "Nobody's perfect," you offer."My record was," she says. "Until today."

It's not until the elevator is in sight that the thought occurs to you. "I didn't break your rules, did I? Even by accident?""No," she says right away. "I'm not some martinet out to punish you on a technicality. Although if you did do something and got away with it, you're cheeky asking about it." She pauses, perhaps considering herself fallible, to see how that would feel. "But I don't think you did. The fault is mine.""Maybe it was a coincidence," you say. You don't believe it, but there's a chance these alien things don't consider probability the way you do."Coincidences are rare. This was close to impossible," she says. Another similarity you can bond over.Maybe you're learning to read her body language after so long with nothing to stare at, because something else occurs to you. "You called them antisocial, paranoid, and arrogant," you say."Yes," she says. She parks within reach of your wheelchair. "If we ever manage to converse, I hope to find the respect is mutual."She helps you back into the elevator without delay.

On the elevator console, there's a small red handset hanging in a cradle beneath the floor buttons. As you look over the buttons, considering your next move, a small bell rings from within the handset.You pick it up gingerly and look into one bulbous end of the crescent. There's a star pattern of speakers within. A tinny voice speaks from it. "Hold it to your ear," says the voice.You press it to your ear. The voice comes through more clearly. It's Joakim's voice. "Now put the other end by your mouth." You do so. "You can reply to me.""Understood," you say."Game night is beginning," he says. "Would you please join the other guests in the VIP Lounge?"

"There's some things I'd like to do. Is it, ah," you say. "Mandatory?""Technically, no," says the automaton. "But I'm going to level with you. You really, really, really, really shouldn't miss it.""I see," you say. "And it has to happen now?""Yes," he says. "It has to happen now."

"I don't think I want to play a game," you say. "I don't want to do Game Night."Joakim is silent for a moment. "I can convey your wishes to the other guests. But I advise against it. Are you sure you can't bring yourself to attend?"

"You know what it sounds like to me," you say. "It sounds like you're trying to lure me into some kind of high stakes scenario that I don't understand, where I do something I regret, because this mixed media reality attaches bizarre significance to," you bite the words, "random stuff."Joakim pauses before answering. "That's an ungenerous rendition of it," he says. "But not far from accurate. I still think it's better than the alternative."

"Which is what?" you ask testily. The elevator doors shut automatically, leaving you to be irate and alone in a small metal box."You'll be returned to your spaceship," says Joakim, "with enough fuel and propellant to get to Sol. Game Night will commence without you."

"Okay, great," you say. "Let me go. Could I have left at any time?""Of course," he says. "You're a guest of 79 AU. You arrived without the fuel reserves to return home, but we will part with it gratis. In case of this dismal scenario, I myself spun up the infrastructure to convert some of our volatiles into useful propellant. It breaks my heart that it might come to pass.""You have gears and cogs for a heart," you say. "Call a mechanic.""I meant only that I would be as sad as I can possibly be," he says.

"You wouldn't be sad. This place isn't a hotel," you say. "None of you are real.""It is a hotel," says Joakim. "It is temporary accommodation for foreigners. What would -" You cut him off."This telephone I'm talking into?" You slam the handset on the safety railing a couple of times. "Not real. The humans that talk about how they're not human and insinuate I'm not either? I'm important but also nobody but also if I don't do what you say I'll fuck up the universe?" you yell into the handset. "BULLSHIT."You notice that you've broken the handset. A voice tries to speak through it, but it is glitchy and barely audible. You fling it against the console. It dangles helplessly beneath. "You can hear me!" you yell at the walls. "I know you can hear me! Let me out! Let me out! Let me out! Let me -"
Crash out until they let you leave

"... out," you say.You're in your pressure suit. In the airlock of your spaceship. Outside the viewport hangs 79 AU, golden, vast, and terrible. Lifetimes ago you went EVA to meet it from this spot.Operating without conscious thought, you retreat from the airlock, close the interior door, and strip out of your spacesuit.Your legs are stiff, and it is harder than usual to maneuver in microgravity. You are ravenously hungry.You take stock of your ship. You have enough fuel to make it home. After pushback, you point the torch drive conspicuously away from 79 AU, and punch it. After you gain some distance, you adjust course back to Sol.

"The game is Bridge," says Joakim. "Head to head, partnerships of two, four players in total." His gold vest, which you know conceals his artificial undercarriage, shines bright. He inclines his head to you, and inclines it opposite to your opponent. Between you, a table. "Once the players have chosen their partners, the game will begin."Despite having found yourself in a new setting, you have no sense of disorientation. In fact, you feel like you know what's going on. Not in specifics; it feels that way. It's like confidence.

The four edges of the game table are lined with green velvet. Underneath is dark walnut wood. It seems positively ancient, and the legs are chipped and scratched, the wear of a true antique. The tablecloth displays a two-dimensional map of planet Earth, drawn in classical style. Around the Earth in unrealistically close orbit are two dozen planetoids, Jupiter most prominently, and a not-big-enough Sol.
